legacy: Donald Broadbent was one of the founders of modern cognitive psychology. He helped shift psychology toward an information-processing approach, treating the mind as a system that receives, filters, and processes information. His theories influenced decades of research on attention, perception, memory, and human performance, providing a foundation for cognitive science and human-computer interaction.
earlyLife: Donald Broadbent was born in Birmingham, England. During his early years he developed interests in science and human behavior. His experiences during military service exposed him to practical problems involving communication, attention, and decision-making in complex environments. These experiences later influenced his scientific interest in understanding how people process information under demanding conditions.
scientificField: Cognitive Psychology, Experimental Psychology, Human Factors Research
majorContributions: Broadbent is best known for developing the Filter Theory of Attention, which proposed that humans selectively process certain information while filtering out other stimuli. His research provided one of the earliest systematic models of attention and information processing. He applied experimental methods to study perception, memory, communication, and decision-making, helping establish cognitive psychology as a rigorous scientific discipline. His work also contributed to human factors research by improving understanding of performance in complex technological environments.
laterLife: Throughout his career, Broadbent continued investigating attention, cognition, and human performance. He collaborated with researchers across psychology and related disciplines, refining theories of information processing and cognitive control. His later work expanded understanding of how humans manage competing sources of information and make decisions in real-world settings.
whyImportant: Donald Broadbent is important because he helped establish the scientific study of attention as a central topic in cognitive psychology. His theories influenced research into learning, perception, memory, communication systems, and human-machine interaction. Many modern investigations into cognition, workload, and information processing build upon concepts that he pioneered.
